title: [Chapitre] VI. Analysis situs (deuxième mouture) : notes manuscrites (18-20/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the second draft ('deuxième mouture') of an axiomatic, combinatorial 'Analysis situs'. It is plausibly connected to the tame-topology programme of Esquisse d'un programme §5, though nothing on this page states that link. The basic data is a set 𝓕 of 'figures' carrying a structure that the previous page calls 'structure d'étalée'.

Previous page: Grothendieck weighed three ways to give this structure: (≤,≪), (≤,≼), or (≪, not-≤). In the first draft he took (≤,≼) as primitive and defined ≪ as the order generated by them, G ≪ F iff G ≤ F' ≼ F for some F'. He found it laborious to derive transitivity and especially reflexivity that way. An added note says that from p. 20 on he changed the rule: ≼ is now to be defined from ≤ and ≪.

This page fixes the choice in (1.30). The primitive data are two order relations ≤ and ≪ on 𝓕, with ≤ ⊂ ≪, i.e. F ≤ G ⇒ F ≪ G. The construction then runs as follows.
1. From these one defines a subset 𝓜 ⊂ 𝓕 by an earlier condition (1.20), with the induced relations ≤_𝓜 and ≪_𝓜. Elements of 𝓜 are presumably 'elementary' or irreducible figures, cell-like; (1.20) is not visible here.
2. One then defines 𝓛 ⊂ 𝓜 by (1.25), plausibly the 'points' or minimal elements.
3. There is a map (*) 𝓕 → 𝓟(𝓜), F ↦ F̃ = Dep(F) = {X ∈ 𝓜 | X ≤ F} (1.31). This is the trace of the principal down-set of F on 𝓜.
4. There is a second map (**) 𝓕 → Fig(𝓜), F ↦ Fig_𝓜(F) = {X̃ | X ∈ F̃} ⊂ 𝓟(𝓜), with X̃ = {Y ∈ 𝓜 | Y ≤ X}, by the earlier formula (1.4). This is the family of 'sub-figures' of F that are elementary, each realised as a subset of 𝓜.

Conclusion: 𝓕 is realised as a family of subsets of 𝓜, and ≤ becomes inclusion (1.32): F ≤ G ⟺ F̃ ⊂ G̃.

In modern terms, this is the standard representation of a poset by a join-dense (more precisely, order-determining) subset: P → down-sets of D, p ↦ ↓p ∩ D. The theme continues in Birkhoff/Priestley-type representations and in the face-poset realisation of regular cell complexes.

The next page explains the price. ≪ has no direct set-theoretic interpretation in terms of the F̃ or of Fig_𝓜(F): G ≪ F does not imply Fig_𝓜(G) ≪ Fig_𝓜(F). Hence the reformulation (1.33): 𝓕 ⊂ 𝓟(M) together with an order ≪ implied by inclusion.

The problem served is choosing the most economical primitive data for an axiomatic theory of 'figures' in a tame or combinatorial topology.
errors: The equivalence (1.32), and the injectivity marked by ↪ in (*), only hold if 𝓜 is order-determining in 𝓕: every F must be determined by the elements of 𝓜 below it, i.e. F ≤ G whenever every X ∈ 𝓜 with X ≤ F satisfies X ≤ G. The direction ⇒ is trivial; the direction ⇐ needs such an axiom, presumably contained in (1.20) or the axioms, but it is not stated on this page.

Fig_𝓜(F) as defined is in canonical bijection with F̃ itself, since X ↦ X̃ is injective under the same hypothesis. So (**) adds no information beyond (*) at the level of sets. Grothendieck himself concedes on the next page that the notation may be 'un peu bidon'.

ideas.what: Taking two nested order relations ≤ ⊂ ≪ on a set of figures as the primitive data of a combinatorial 'analysis situs', instead of defining ≪ from ≤ and a refinement relation ≼
ideas.modern_name: axiomatic tame topology / poset-based combinatorial topology (closest: face posets, stratified-space posets)
ideas.usually_credited_to: tame topology programme: Grothendieck (Esquisse, 1984); o-minimality: van den Dries, Pillay–Steinhorn, Knight
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme §5 only sketches 'topologie modérée'; this specific axiomatics with (≤,≪) appears unpublished

ideas.what: Embedding of 𝓕 into 𝓟(𝓜) via F ↦ {X ∈ 𝓜 | X ≤ F}, turning ≤ into inclusion
ideas.modern_name: representation of a poset by down-sets of a join-dense / order-determining subset (Birkhoff-type representation)

ideas.what: Fig_𝓜(F): the family of elementary sub-figures X̃ of F, each realised as a subset of 𝓜
ideas.modern_name: family of closed cells of a cell complex, viewed as subsets of its face poset
ideas.usually_credited_to: standard in combinatorial topology (face poset of a regular CW complex)

missed.claim: The page records Grothendieck's design decision for an axiomatic tame topology. The two orders ≤ ⊂ ≪ are primitive and a refinement relation ≼ is derived from them, reversing the first draft. He also notes, on the next page, that ≪ has no set-theoretic interpretation once figures are realised as subsets of the elementary figures 𝓜. The intended full axiomatics (with 𝓜 and 𝓛 defined by (1.20) and (1.25)) appears never to have been published or taken up. However, nothing on this page by itself is a result.
missed.quote: C'est donc de deux relations d'ordre (1.30) ≤ , ≪ ... telles que F≤G ⇒ F≪G que je vais partir.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is of minor interest for the history of Grothendieck's tame-topology programme, and as an alternative, purely order-theoretic axiomatisation that could be compared with o-minimal cell decomposition or with poset models of stratified spaces (exit-path posets). The mathematics on this page itself is routine.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a transitional page that records a choice of primitive data. The only construction is a routine down-set representation of a poset. Its interest is archival, as part of the unpublished 'Analysis situs' axiomatics, rather than as a new result.
transcription_corrections: Line 1–2: 'En résumé, en termes de 𝓕, ainsi de ce domaine de deux relations d'ordre' should read 'En résumé, en termes de 𝓕, c'est donc de deux relations d'ordre'. Together with 'que je vais partir', the sentence is 'c'est ... de deux relations d'ordre ... que je vais partir'.
The second map is labelled (**) in the image, written like '(✱✱)'; the first is (*), drawn as a star.
'Dep[?](F)' looks like 'Dep(F)' (possibly 'Dép'); the reading is uncertain.
The struck '(1.32)' next to the Fig formula is confirmed. The final (1.32) is the inclusion equivalence, where the second tilde in the image is drawn as a breve over G (G̃).
